site.name: HTML Tools
site.description: Free, browser-based developer tools — format JSON, test regex, compress images, generate gradients, and more. No installs, no servers, no tracking.

tools.name: JSON Formatter
tools.card: Prettify, minify, and validate JSON with syntax highlighting.
tools.description: Format, validate, and minify JSON with syntax highlighting and a collapsible tree view. Runs in your browser — no installs, no servers, no tracking.

faqs.q: Is JSON Formatter free?
faqs.a: Yes. Every tool here runs entirely in your browser — no accounts, no quotas, no rate limits.

faqs.q: Does my JSON ever leave my computer?
faqs.a: No. The page is a single static HTML file; all parsing and formatting happen locally in your browser.

faqs.q: What's the difference between Format and Minify?
faqs.a: Format pretty-prints with two-space indentation for readability. Minify strips whitespace and newlines so the output is the smallest valid JSON.

faqs.q: Can I search through formatted output?
faqs.a: Yes. Press Ctrl/Cmd+F to open an inline search that highlights matches across keys and values, even inside the collapsible tree view.

tools.name: JSON to TypeScript
tools.card: Convert JSON objects into TypeScript interface definitions.
tools.description: Convert JSON to TypeScript interfaces or type aliases — handles optional fields, mixed arrays, and nested objects. Runs in your browser, no tracking.

faqs.q: Should I use interface or type?
faqs.a: Either — toggle in the UI. Interfaces are easier to extend; type aliases compose better via unions and intersections.

faqs.q: Why are some fields marked optional (?:)?
faqs.a: If a field is missing in any element of an array, the generator marks it optional so the resulting type matches every element.

faqs.q: How are mixed-type arrays handled?
faqs.a: They're emitted as a union — for example, an array containing strings and numbers becomes (string | number)[].

faqs.q: Does it handle deeply nested objects?
faqs.a: Yes. Nested objects are flattened into a list of named interfaces so the output stays readable instead of one massive type.

tools.name: JSON Diff
tools.card: Compare two JSON objects and highlight the differences.
tools.description: Compare two JSON objects and instantly see what was added, removed, or changed. Runs in your browser — no installs, no servers, no tracking.

faqs.q: Will whitespace or key-order differences show up?
faqs.a: No. Both inputs are normalized before diffing, so only real structural differences are highlighted.

faqs.q: How are arrays compared?
faqs.a: By index. Reordering an array shows up as a removal-then-addition pair. Use JSON Sort first if you want order-insensitive comparison.

faqs.q: Can it handle large JSON files?
faqs.a: Anything that fits comfortably in your browser memory. There's no hard limit; the diff updates as you type.

faqs.q: Are there really no servers involved?
faqs.a: Right. The page is a single static HTML file; the comparison happens entirely in your browser.

tools.name: JSON Sort
tools.card: Sort JSON object keys alphabetically (A→Z or Z→A), recursively.
tools.description: Sort JSON object keys alphabetically (A→Z or Z→A) recursively, for canonical, line-stable output. Runs in your browser — no installs, no tracking.

faqs.q: Will it sort arrays too?
faqs.a: No. Only object keys are sorted; arrays preserve their original order, since array order is usually meaningful.

faqs.q: Does the output stay valid JSON?
faqs.a: Yes. Lenient input quirks like trailing commas or comments are dropped; the output is always strict JSON.

faqs.q: Why would I sort JSON keys?
faqs.a: It produces canonical output for line-stable git diffs, repeatable fingerprints, and easier visual comparison of objects with the same shape.

faqs.q: Is sorting recursive?
faqs.a: Yes. Every nested object in the tree is sorted in one pass.

tools.name: JSON ↔ CSV
tools.card: Round-trip JSON and CSV with smart type inference and delimiter detection.
tools.description: Convert between JSON and CSV — RFC 4180 quoting, type inference, configurable delimiters. Runs in your browser — no installs, no servers, no tracking.

faqs.q: How are nested JSON objects handled?
faqs.a: Flattened to dot-path columns by default (so address.city becomes its own column). Switch to underscore or JSON-literal modes if you'd rather keep them whole.

faqs.q: How are arrays inside objects handled?
faqs.a: Joined with commas by default — for example ["red","blue"] becomes "red,blue" — or kept as JSON literals via the option toggle.

faqs.q: Why are numbers in my CSV becoming strings?
faqs.a: Type inference is on by default. Make sure the value isn't surrounded by extra whitespace or quoted twice. Switch to off if you want exact CSV → JSON.string round-trip.

faqs.q: Does it auto-detect the delimiter?
faqs.a: Yes for CSV → JSON. The detector samples the first ~10 lines and picks whichever of comma, semicolon, tab, or pipe produces the most consistent column count.

faqs.q: Will the CSV preserve quotes and commas in cell values?
faqs.a: Yes. RFC 4180 quoting is applied automatically: cells with the delimiter, a double-quote, or a newline get quoted, and any internal double-quote is doubled.

tools.name: JSON ↔ YAML
tools.card: Round-trip JSON and YAML with anchor resolution and multi-document support.
tools.description: Convert between JSON and YAML — YAML 1.2, anchors, aliases, and multi-document support. Runs in your browser — no installs, no servers, no tracking.

faqs.q: Are comments preserved when converting YAML to JSON?
faqs.a: No. JSON has no comment syntax, so they're dropped. The status bar shows a count of how many were stripped so you don't lose them silently.

faqs.q: How are anchors and aliases handled?
faqs.a: Resolved into duplicated values when going to JSON. Going JSON → YAML doesn't reintroduce anchors automatically; if you need DRY YAML, edit by hand after.

faqs.q: Does it support multi-document YAML (`---`)?
faqs.a: Yes. Choose between first doc only (default) and array of docs (each doc becomes one element of a top-level JSON array).

faqs.q: Why is `yes` not converting to `true`?
faqs.a: That's a YAML 1.1 quirk. We follow YAML 1.2 by default, where only `true`/`false` (and a few variants) are booleans. `yes`/`no` stay as strings.

faqs.q: What's the difference between block and flow style?
faqs.a: Block uses indentation and dashes — the typical outline-style YAML look. Flow looks more like JSON: `{key: value, list: [a, b]}`. Auto picks block for larger structures and flow for short inline ones.

tools.name: JSON to Validator Schema
tools.card: Generate Zod, Valibot, or Yup schemas from a JSON sample.
tools.description: Paste a JSON sample and get runtime-validation schemas for Zod, Valibot, and Yup — optional field detection, null handling, and strict mode. Runs in your browser — no installs, no tracking.

faqs.q: Which validators are supported?
faqs.a: Zod, Valibot, and Yup. All three outputs are generated from a single inference pass — switching tabs doesn't re-parse the input.

faqs.q: How are optional fields detected?
faqs.a: If a key is missing in any element of an array of objects, the generator marks that key as optional — the same heuristic used by the JSON to TypeScript tool. Top-level keys are required unless null and the 'Treat null as optional' toggle is on.

faqs.q: What does 'Treat null as optional' do?
faqs.a: When on, any field whose value is null gets wrapped in the validator's nullable modifier — .nullable() for Zod/Yup, v.nullable() for Valibot — making it accept both the typed value and null.

faqs.q: What does 'Strict mode' do?
faqs.a: Strict mode rejects unknown keys on objects: .strict() in Zod, v.strictObject() in Valibot, .noUnknown(true) in Yup. Useful when you want the schema to be an exact shape contract rather than a minimum requirement.

faqs.q: How are mixed-type arrays handled?
faqs.a: The element types are collected and wrapped in a union — z.array(z.union([…])) for Zod, v.array(v.union([…])) for Valibot. Yup doesn't have first-class union support, so mixed arrays emit yup.array() without a typed element.

tools.name: Regex Tester
tools.card: Test JavaScript regular expressions live with capture-group breakdown.
tools.description: Test JavaScript regex live — match, replace, split; flag toggles; capture groups; cheat sheet. Runs in your browser — no installs, no servers, no tracking.

faqs.q: Which regex flavor does this use?
faqs.a: JavaScript's built-in RegExp (the same engine your browser runs). It's close to PCRE but not identical — features like atomic groups, recursion, and possessive quantifiers don't exist here.

faqs.q: Why is my regex matching nothing?
faqs.a: Most often: the g flag is off (so only the first match shows), or the pattern is anchored to the start (^) or end ($) without m, or character classes need escaping. Check the flag pills and the cheat sheet at the bottom.

faqs.q: What does the d flag do?
faqs.a: It exposes the start/end indices of each capture group. Without it you only get the matched text; with it you get exact positions.

faqs.q: Can I test against a huge file?
faqs.a: Anything that fits in your browser memory. The status bar warns if a run exceeds 200ms, which usually means catastrophic backtracking — try rewriting nested quantifiers.

faqs.q: Are my regex and test text saved anywhere?
faqs.a: No. The page is a single static HTML file; nothing leaves your browser. We don't even persist to localStorage.

tools.name: SVG to JSX
tools.card: Convert SVG markup into React JSX-compatible component code.
tools.description: Convert SVG markup to React JSX — camelCase attributes, className, inline style objects. Runs in your browser — no installs, no servers, no tracking.

faqs.q: What gets transformed?
faqs.a: Kebab-case attributes become camelCase, class becomes className, inline styles become objects, and editor metadata (like XML declarations and comments) is stripped.

faqs.q: Does it preserve viewBox and other SVG-specific attributes?
faqs.a: Yes. Attributes that JSX expects in camelCase — viewBox, preserveAspectRatio, clipPath, etc. — are converted correctly.

faqs.q: Can I drop the result straight into a React component?
faqs.a: Yes. The output is JSX you can paste directly into a function component or wrap in a generated component template.

faqs.q: How do I make the icon use my theme color?
faqs.a: After copying, replace fill or stroke values with currentColor so the icon picks up the surrounding text color via CSS.

tools.name: SVG to Raster
tools.card: Rasterize an SVG to PNG, JPEG, or WebP at any pixel size — preset sizes, aspect lock.
tools.description: Paste or drop an SVG and export it as PNG, JPEG, or WebP at any pixel size — preset social-card dimensions, aspect-ratio lock, quality slider, copy to clipboard. Runs in your browser — no installs, no servers, no tracking.

faqs.q: How is this different from SVG to JSX?
faqs.a: SVG to JSX rewrites the markup for React (camelCase props, className) but keeps the result as SVG code. SVG to Raster renders the SVG to actual pixels — a PNG, JPEG, or WebP image — at the exact dimensions you ask for.

faqs.q: How does it know the SVG's natural size?
faqs.a: The parser reads the root <svg>'s width and height attributes first, falling back to the viewBox if either is missing. If none of those are present, it defaults to 300×150 (which is what browsers use for an SVG with no dimensions).

faqs.q: What does Lock aspect do?
faqs.a: When the source SVG has known dimensions, editing one of W or H auto-fills the other so the ratio matches the source. Presets ignore the lock so they always set both dimensions, since their whole point is to enforce a specific ratio.

faqs.q: Why is the exported image blank or missing parts?
faqs.a: The canvas pipeline can't fetch external assets — fonts referenced via @import or <link>, <image href> pointing at a different origin, and external stylesheets all silently fail. Inline fonts as glyph paths and embed images as data URIs.

faqs.q: Does the SVG ever leave my browser?
faqs.a: No. Parsing, rendering, and encoding all run locally — the SVG only ever becomes a Blob URL that gets painted onto a canvas, never a network request.

tools.name: Gradients
tools.card: Curated gradient collection — copy CSS, Tailwind, or export PNG.
tools.description: Browse 87 curated gradients and copy as CSS, Tailwind classes, or PNG export. Runs in your browser — no installs, no servers, no tracking.

faqs.q: Where do these gradients come from?
faqs.a: Hand-curated for typical UI use cases — heroes, banners, accent surfaces — with an eye on contrast and readability over text.

faqs.q: Are the Tailwind classes v3 or v4?
faqs.a: The output uses bg-gradient-to-* with from-/via-/to- color stops, which both Tailwind v3 and v4 support.

faqs.q: What size are the PNG exports?
faqs.a: 1200×630, sized for OG and Twitter cards. Drop them straight into a meta tag or social preview without resizing.

faqs.q: Can I customize the colors?
faqs.a: The gallery itself is fixed, but the CSS output is a regular linear-gradient — copy it and tweak the stops, angle, or color space.

tools.name: Blob Generator
tools.card: Generate organic blob shapes — CSS border-radius or SVG path.
tools.description: Generate organic blob shapes with CSS border-radius or SVG paths — copy, animate, or download. Runs in your browser, no installs, no tracking.

faqs.q: Should I use CSS or SVG mode?
faqs.a: CSS for static decorative shapes — no SVG required, works in every modern browser. SVG when you need a path you can animate, mask, or further edit.

faqs.q: Does the CSS version work everywhere?
faqs.a: Yes. The 8-value border-radius syntax is part of the CSS spec and supported in every modern browser.

faqs.q: Can I animate the blob?
faqs.a: Yes. The CSS version animates by transitioning the border-radius values; the SVG path can be tweened with CSS or any animation library.

faqs.q: What's Catmull-Rom?
faqs.a: A spline-fitting algorithm that produces smooth curves through a set of control points. SVG mode uses it so blobs look organic instead of polygonal.

tools.name: Image Compressor
tools.card: Compress PNG, JPEG, WebP, and AVIF images — quality presets or target size in KB.
tools.description: Compress PNG, JPEG, WebP, and AVIF images — quality presets or target-size (KB budget). Runs in your browser — no installs, no servers, no tracking.

faqs.q: Does my image ever leave my computer?
faqs.a: No. Everything happens locally in your browser — no upload, no server, no third-party API. Decoding and encoding run in a Web Worker.

faqs.q: What's the difference between this and the Image Format Converter?
faqs.a: The converter is about format choice (PNG → WebP, etc.). The compressor is about hitting a size target — pick a preset, or specify a KB budget and we binary-search the quality for you.

faqs.q: How does target-size mode work?
faqs.a: We re-encode the image with different quality values and binary-search until the output falls inside your target ± tolerance (default ±5%). Up to 8 iterations per file; we surface the final quality and iteration count.

faqs.q: What if my target size isn't achievable?
faqs.a: We surface the smallest size we managed and flag the card with "target not hit." Common cause: a giant photo at a too-aggressive target — tick "Resize first" to shrink the input before encoding.

faqs.q: What does 'Lossless' actually mean here?
faqs.a: PNG output — pixel-identical to the source, just with PNG's compression. The quality slider doesn't apply. (Canvas-based WebP-lossless isn't exposed by browsers, so PNG is the only true-lossless option in this tool.)

faqs.q: Why is my output sometimes bigger than the input?
faqs.a: Re-encoding already-compressed lossy formats can grow the file (the source was already aggressive). The summary bar flags this in red so you don't accidentally ship a worse copy — keep the original in that case.

tools.name: Image Resizer
tools.card: Batch-resize images by percentage, exact size, or max dimensions — social-card presets.
tools.description: Batch-resize images by percentage, exact size, or max dimensions — social-card presets, zip download. Runs in your browser, no installs, no tracking.

faqs.q: Does my image ever leave my computer?
faqs.a: No. Everything runs locally in your browser — decoding, resizing, and encoding all happen on-device via a Web Worker.

faqs.q: What's the difference between Percentage, Exact, and Max?
faqs.a: Percentage scales every image by the same factor — quick "halve everything" workflows. Exact forces every output to a specific W × H and center-crops to fill — useful for social cards (OG 1200×630, Twitter 1600×900, etc.). Max caps the longer side while keeping the source aspect — good for blog images where you want "max 1600px wide" without distorting.

faqs.q: What does Lock aspect ratio do?
faqs.a: In Max mode it preserves the source's aspect while fitting inside your max W × max H. In Exact mode it captures the current W:H when toggled on — editing one dimension then auto-fills the other so the captured ratio stays constant. Default is on in both modes.

faqs.q: Will the resizer upscale a small image?
faqs.a: Max and Percentage modes are shrink-only — they never produce output larger than the source (Percentage's slider caps at 100% for the same reason). Exact mode returns whatever W × H you set, including dimensions larger than the source — the result will just look fuzzier.

faqs.q: Where did the presets go?
faqs.a: Presets (OG 1200×630, Twitter 1600×900, Half, Quarter, Thumb 256) only appear when Lock aspect ratio is off in Max or Exact mode — they set explicit dimensions, which would otherwise silently violate the locked ratio. Percentage mode is implicitly always locked, so presets don't appear there.

faqs.q: Can I download all my resized images at once?
faqs.a: Yes. The Download all (zip) button packs every output into a single store-only zip — unpacking is instant. Each row's Download button gets a single file.

faqs.q: Why are some files marked 'kept original'?
faqs.a: If the source is already at or below the target and the format isn't changing, we skip the re-encode so you don't lose quality for no benefit. The file goes into the zip verbatim.

tools.name: Image Cropper
tools.card: Crop a region — rectangle or circle, drag the box, lock an aspect ratio.
tools.description: Crop any image to a region — rectangle or circle, aspect-ratio presets, keyboard nudge. Runs in your browser — no installs, no servers, no tracking.

faqs.q: Does my image ever leave my computer?
faqs.a: No. Cropping and encoding both happen locally in your browser via a Web Worker — nothing is uploaded.

faqs.q: Can I crop multiple images at once?
faqs.a: No — cropping is per-image because you're picking a region by hand. For bulk pixel changes that don't need manual framing, see the resizer or compressor.

faqs.q: How do I lock to a square (or other) aspect ratio?
faqs.a: Pick a ratio in the toolbar — 1:1, 4:3, 3:2, 16:9, 9:16, the original ratio of the source, or a custom W:H pair. Edge handles disappear when a ratio is locked; only corners are draggable.

faqs.q: Can I crop to a circle (e.g. for a round avatar)?
faqs.a: Yes — switch the Shape control to Circle. The bounding box stays square (we force 1:1) and the corners outside the inscribed circle are rendered transparent. Output goes to PNG or WebP so the alpha is preserved; JPEG is disabled in circle mode.

faqs.q: Will the orientation of my iPhone photo be respected?
faqs.a: Yes — we read the EXIF orientation flag when decoding so portrait photos don't crop sideways.

faqs.q: What about animated GIFs?
faqs.a: We crop the first frame only. If you need to crop every frame, that's a different tool — we don't support it here.

tools.name: Image Format Converter
tools.card: Convert images between PNG, JPEG, WebP, and AVIF with a quality slider and before/after diff.
tools.description: Convert images between PNG, JPEG, WebP, and AVIF with a quality slider and before/after diff. Runs in your browser — no installs, no servers, no tracking.

faqs.q: Does my image ever leave my computer?
faqs.a: No. Decoding, conversion, and download all happen in your browser — nothing is uploaded.

faqs.q: Which formats can I convert between?
faqs.a: Input: PNG, JPEG, WebP, AVIF, GIF, BMP. Output: PNG, JPEG, WebP, AVIF. AVIF encoding requires a recent browser (Chrome/Edge 121+, Firefox 116+, Safari 16.4+); the pill is disabled if your browser can't do it.

faqs.q: Why is the quality slider disabled for PNG output?
faqs.a: PNG is lossless — there's no quality knob to turn. Use WebP or AVIF if you want to trade quality for size.

faqs.q: What happens to animated GIFs?
faqs.a: Only the first frame is converted. Multi-frame output isn't supported here; if you need animation, keep the original.

faqs.q: Are EXIF and color profiles preserved?
faqs.a: No. The Canvas pipeline strips EXIF/IPTC and converts to sRGB. That's a privacy plus for sharing photos but worth knowing if you rely on a wide-gamut color profile.

tools.name: Meta Tag Preview
tools.card: See how your URL looks as a Twitter, Facebook, LinkedIn, and Google card.
tools.description: Preview how a URL or HTML snippet renders as a Google, Twitter, Facebook, LinkedIn, WhatsApp, or Telegram card. Runs in your browser, no tracking.

faqs.q: Does pasting a URL send my data to a third party?
faqs.a: Yes — when you use URL mode, the URL is forwarded to a public CORS proxy (oge.vercel.app) that fetches the page server-side. Raw HTML mode parses entirely in your browser with no network request.

faqs.q: Why does the tool use a proxy instead of fetching directly?
faqs.a: Browsers block cross-origin requests to arbitrary sites (CORS policy). A server-side proxy fetches the page for you and returns the meta data as JSON.

faqs.q: Which meta tags are extracted?
faqs.a: Open Graph (og:title, og:description, og:image, og:url), Twitter Card (twitter:card, twitter:title, twitter:description, twitter:image), the plain <title> tag, meta description, canonical URL, robots, and viewport.

faqs.q: What is twitter:card and why does it change the preview?
faqs.a: twitter:card controls the card layout Twitter uses: 'summary' shows a small thumbnail beside the text, while 'summary_large_image' shows a full-width banner image above the text.

faqs.q: Why is the image not showing in the preview?
faqs.a: The image URL must be absolute (https://…) and publicly accessible. Relative URLs, data URIs, and images behind authentication won't load in the preview.

tools.name: Cron Decoder
tools.card: Decode a cron expression into plain English and preview the next 10 run times.
tools.description: Decode a cron expression into plain English with the next 10 run times, or build one field by field. Runs in your browser — no installs, no tracking.

faqs.q: Which cron syntax does this support?
faqs.a: Standard Vixie / Unix cron: 5 fields (minute, hour, day-of-month, month, day-of-week) or 6 fields with a leading seconds field. * (every), */n (step), a-b (range), a,b,c (list), names like MON or JAN, and the @hourly / @daily / @weekly / @monthly / @yearly shortcuts are all parsed.

faqs.q: Are the next-run times in my local timezone?
faqs.a: Yes. Times are computed in your browser using the local Date object, so the schedule reflects the timezone of the device you're viewing the page on. Servers usually evaluate cron in UTC — keep that in mind when sanity-checking a production schedule.

faqs.q: What about L, W, and # (extended syntax)?
faqs.a: L (last), W (nearest weekday) and # (nth-weekday of month) are best-effort. The expression still parses, but the human description and the next-runs list flag it as approximate so you don't trust the preview blindly.

faqs.q: Why does day-of-month and day-of-week behave oddly together?
faqs.a: When both fields are constrained (neither is *), Vixie cron triggers when either matches (OR, not AND). The next-runs list follows that rule, so 0 0 1 * MON fires on every Monday and the 1st of the month.

faqs.q: Does any of this hit a server?
faqs.a: No. Parsing, the human description, and the next-runs computation all run locally in your browser. The page is a single static HTML file.

tools.name: User Agent Parser
tools.card: Break a UA string down into browser, engine, OS, device type, and CPU.
tools.description: Paste a user-agent string and instantly see the browser, engine, OS, device type, and CPU architecture. Runs in your browser — no installs, no tracking.

faqs.q: Where does the pre-filled UA string come from?
faqs.a: It's your own browser's navigator.userAgent — the exact value any website you visit would see. Edit it to test other UAs.

faqs.q: Why does Chrome on iOS show up as CriOS / 'Chrome (iOS)'?
faqs.a: Apple requires every browser on iOS to use WebKit. CriOS / FxiOS / EdgiOS are the tokens Chrome / Firefox / Edge add on iOS so servers can still distinguish them, even though the engine is WebKit underneath.

faqs.q: Can it tell Windows 10 apart from Windows 11?
faqs.a: Not reliably — Microsoft kept the UA at "Windows NT 10.0" for both. The tool shows "Windows 10/11" for that NT version. UA Client Hints (Sec-CH-UA-Platform-Version) can distinguish them, but those aren't present in a plain UA string.

faqs.q: Is the parser 100% accurate?
faqs.a: UA strings are best-effort by design — browsers spoof each other for compatibility (Chrome includes 'Safari', Edge includes 'Chrome', etc.). The parser uses the priority order most servers do, but for high-stakes detection prefer UA Client Hints or feature detection.

faqs.q: Does my UA string leave my computer?
faqs.a: No. Parsing happens entirely in your browser — the page is a single static HTML file with no network requests.

tools.name: OG Image Builder
tools.card: Design a 1200×630 social card — title, subtitle, gradient, logo — export as PNG.
tools.description: Design a 1200×630 Open Graph image with title, subtitle, gradient background, and logo — export as PNG. Runs in your browser, no tracking.

faqs.q: What's an Open Graph image and why does size matter?
faqs.a: It's the preview image social platforms (Facebook, LinkedIn, X/Twitter, Slack, Discord, …) show when someone shares your link. 1200×630 is the standard Open Graph and Twitter summary-large-image size — using it avoids cropping or pixelation across platforms.

faqs.q: Does my image ever leave my browser?
faqs.a: No. The canvas is rendered locally and exported via canvas.toBlob — there's no upload, no server, no third-party API. Even the logo you drop in is read with FileReader and never transmitted.

faqs.q: Why are only a few fonts offered?
faqs.a: Canvas can only render fonts the device has installed (or that this page loads). We expose the two web-fonts this site already ships (Bricolage Grotesque, IBM Plex Mono) plus Georgia (universally installed) so the exported PNG matches the preview on every machine.

faqs.q: What does 'auto-shrink' do to long titles?
faqs.a: If a title overflows the safe area (60 px inset on all sides), the renderer steps the font size down in 4 px increments until it fits or hits a sensible minimum. For very long titles, also enable word-wrap or split with a manual line break.

faqs.q: Why might Copy image fail?
faqs.a: Browsers only allow image clipboard writes from a user gesture, and only on https / localhost. Firefox in particular gates image/png clipboard writes behind a flag in older releases. If the copy fails, use Download PNG — it works everywhere.

tools.name: Wave Generator
tools.card: Generate SVG wave dividers — single wave or stacked layers.
tools.description: Generate SVG wave dividers — single or stacked layers with custom amplitude, frequency, and gradient fill. Runs in your browser, no tracking.

faqs.q: How do I make the wave responsive?
faqs.a: Drop the SVG into a width:100% container; the viewBox scales fluidly with the parent.

faqs.q: Can I stack multiple waves?
faqs.a: Yes. Stacked mode lets you set layer count, vertical spacing, and color interpolation between two endpoints.

faqs.q: Will the gradient fill render in all browsers?
faqs.a: Yes. SVG gradient fills have universal support across every modern browser, including mobile.

faqs.q: Sweeping curves vs. choppy waves — how?
faqs.a: Lower frequency for sweeping, gentle curves; higher frequency for choppy, sea-style waves. Amplitude controls how tall the peaks are.

tools.name: Code Snippet to Image
tools.card: Turn code into a sharable PNG card with VS Code-grade syntax highlighting.
tools.description: Turn a code snippet into a sharable PNG card — paste code, pick a language and a VS Code theme, tweak window chrome and padding, export as PNG. Runs in your browser, no tracking.

faqs.q: Does my code ever leave my browser?
faqs.a: No. Tokenization (via Shiki and a JavaScript regex engine), canvas layout, and PNG encoding all run locally. There's no upload, no server, no third-party API.

faqs.q: Why does my snippet look identical to VS Code?
faqs.a: We use Shiki, which uses the same TextMate grammars and theme JSON files that VS Code uses. The colors and tokenization match VS Code byte-for-byte.

faqs.q: Why does switching to a new language or theme briefly show a spinner?
faqs.a: Each grammar and theme is a separate file loaded on demand to keep the initial page small. Once loaded they're cached in memory for the rest of the session.

faqs.q: Why is my language not on the list?
faqs.a: We ship a curated set of grammars to keep the page light. Open an issue on GitHub and we'll add it.

faqs.q: Can I export with a transparent background?
faqs.a: Yes — pick Transparent under Background. The PNG is saved with an alpha channel so the card sits on whatever surface you drop it on.

tools.name: Text Diff
tools.card: Compare two plain-text blocks line-by-line with word-level inline highlighting.
tools.description: Compare two plain-text inputs line-by-line with word-level inline highlighting, split view, line numbers, and scroll sync. Runs in your browser — no installs, no tracking.

faqs.q: How is this different from JSON Diff?
faqs.a: JSON Diff understands JSON structure — it compares keys, values, and nested objects semantically. Text Diff is format-agnostic: it diffs any two plain-text files line by line, so it works on code, prose, config files, or anything else.

faqs.q: What does 'Ignore whitespace' do?
faqs.a: When checked, leading and trailing whitespace on each line is trimmed before comparing. A line that only changed indentation won't show as modified.

faqs.q: What does 'Show unchanged lines' do?
faqs.a: By default only changed lines are shown (like git diff --unified=0). Enabling this option also renders unchanged context lines between hunks so you can see where each change sits.

faqs.q: What format does 'Copy diff' produce?
faqs.a: A plain +/- prefixed text block: lines prefixed with + were added, - were removed, and unchanged context lines (if shown) have no prefix. It's human-readable without any special tooling.

faqs.q: Does any text leave my browser?
faqs.a: No. The comparison runs entirely in your browser using a vanilla-JS LCS algorithm — there's no upload, no server, no network request of any kind.

tools.name: QR Code Generator
tools.card: Turn any text, URL, WiFi config, or vCard into a QR code — export as SVG or PNG.
tools.description: Turn any text, URL, WiFi config, or vCard into a QR code. Customize colors and error-correction level, then download as SVG or PNG.

faqs.q: Does my data ever leave my browser?
faqs.a: No. Encoding, SVG rendering, and PNG export all happen locally in your browser via an inlined version of Project Nayuki's QR encoder (MIT). No upload, no server, no CDN call.

faqs.q: What does the error-correction level (L/M/Q/H) actually do?
faqs.a: QR codes carry redundant data so they still scan when partially damaged or obscured. L tolerates ~7% damage, M ~15%, Q ~25%, H ~30%. Higher levels need more space, so the same payload fits less easily — pick L for the densest code, H if you're overlaying a logo or printing on glossy material.

faqs.q: Why do I get "content exceeds capacity" on long input?
faqs.a: The chosen error-correction level reserves a percentage of the code for recovery data. Lower it (H → L) to fit more, shorten the payload, or remember that URLs encode much smaller than free-form text because the alphanumeric mode is restricted to 0-9 A-Z space $ % * + - . / :.

faqs.q: Will a centered logo still scan?
faqs.a: Usually yes if the logo covers under ~20% of the code area and you've used error-correction H (which is auto-selected when you add a logo). Test on a real phone before printing — the tool warns when a logo gets large enough to risk readability.

faqs.q: Should I export as SVG or PNG?
faqs.a: SVG for anything that will be resized, printed, or embedded in a webpage — it scales infinitely and stays crisp. PNG when you need a flat raster file (e.g. attaching to a chat message); pick 1024 px if you're printing, 256/512 px for screen use.

tools.name: Lorem Ipsum Generator
tools.card: Generate placeholder text — paragraphs, sentences, words, or list items, with flavored dictionaries.
tools.description: Generate Lorem Ipsum placeholder text — paragraphs, sentences, words, or list items, with Cupcake / Bacon / Hipster dictionaries too. Runs in your browser — no installs, no tracking.

faqs.q: What does 'lorem ipsum' actually mean?
faqs.a: It's scrambled Latin adapted from Cicero's De finibus bonorum et malorum (45 BC), used as printer's filler since the 1500s. Designers reach for it because the unfamiliar letterforms keep the eye on layout instead of meaning.

faqs.q: Why are there alternative dictionaries (Cupcake, Bacon, Hipster)?
faqs.a: Same purpose, more fun. Cupcake leans dessert words, Bacon leans meat words, Hipster leans artisanal-coffee-shop nouns. Pick whichever fits the vibe of what you're mocking up.

faqs.q: Will the first paragraph always start with 'Lorem ipsum dolor sit amet…'?
faqs.a: Only when the dictionary is set to Lorem and the 'Start with classic intro' toggle is on (both are the default). Turn it off if you want a fully random first sentence.

faqs.q: Can I paste this into production copy?
faqs.a: No — it's nonsense Latin (or nonsense English). Treat it as a layout-only placeholder; replace it with real copy before shipping.

faqs.q: Does my generated text ever leave my computer?
faqs.a: No. The page is a single static HTML file; all generation happens locally in your browser with no network requests.

tools.name: Markdown Preview
tools.card: Live Markdown editor with GFM support — tables, task lists, strikethrough.
tools.description: Paste or type Markdown and see a live rendered preview — CommonMark + GitHub Flavored Markdown (tables, task lists, strikethrough). Runs in your browser, no tracking.

faqs.q: Which Markdown flavour does the preview support?
faqs.a: CommonMark plus GitHub Flavored Markdown (GFM) — tables, task-list checkboxes, strikethrough, and fenced code blocks with a language hint.

faqs.q: Does my Markdown ever leave my browser?
faqs.a: No. Parsing and rendering happen entirely in your browser using the marked library bundled with the page — no upload, no server, no network request of any kind.

faqs.q: Can I copy the rendered HTML?
faqs.a: Yes — click 'Copy HTML' to put the rendered HTML string on your clipboard. Click 'Copy Markdown' to copy the raw source instead.

faqs.q: Will links in the preview navigate away from the tool?
faqs.a: No. Every link in the rendered preview opens in a new tab so you stay on the tool.

faqs.q: How do I save my Markdown?
faqs.a: Click '⬇️ Download .md' to save the editor content as a .md file. Your browser handles the download — nothing is sent to a server.

tools.name: Avatar Generator
tools.card: Generate an initial-based avatar from a name — choose shape, style, and export as PNG.
tools.description: Generate an avatar from a name — auto-extracts initials, picks a deterministic color, choose shape and style, export as PNG. All in your browser, no tracking.

faqs.q: How are initials extracted from the name?
faqs.a: The tool takes the first letter of the first word and the first letter of the last word (uppercased), giving you up to 2 characters. You can override them in the Initials field.

faqs.q: How is the avatar color chosen automatically?
faqs.a: A simple hash of the name string deterministically picks one of 8 preset colors, so the same name always produces the same color — no random flickering on reload.

faqs.q: Does the image ever leave my browser?
faqs.a: No. All rendering happens on a <canvas> element in your browser. Nothing is uploaded. The PNG download and clipboard copy are both generated locally.

faqs.q: What's the difference between Gradient, Flat, and Outlined styles?
faqs.a: Gradient fills the background with a two-tone linear gradient. Flat uses a solid fill. Outlined leaves the background transparent and draws a border plus initials in the chosen color.

faqs.q: Why does clipboard copy sometimes fail?
faqs.a: Clipboard access requires a secure context (HTTPS or localhost) and a user gesture. If it fails, use the Download button instead — the PNG is identical.

tools.name: Favicon Generator
tools.card: Drop an image or pick an emoji to generate a full favicon set — PNG, ICO, maskable, manifest.
tools.description: Drop any image or type an emoji to generate the full browser favicon set — 16/32/48/180/192/512 PNGs, a multi-frame favicon.ico, a maskable variant, and a manifest.webmanifest snippet, all bundled into one zip. Runs in your browser, no tracking.

faqs.q: Which sizes are in the exported zip?
faqs.a: 16×16, 32×32, 48×48, 180×180 (Apple touch icon), 192×192 and 512×512 (Android chrome). Plus a two-frame favicon.ico (16+32 px), a 512×512 maskable variant, and a manifest.webmanifest snippet referencing the manifest icons.

faqs.q: What is a maskable icon?
faqs.a: On Android and other adaptive-icon platforms, the OS clips the icon to a shape (circle, squircle, teardrop, …). Maskable icons fill the canvas with background + foreground and keep the meaningful content inside the inner 60% (a 20% safe-area padding on each side) so cropping never removes it.

faqs.q: Does the tool use a real ICO encoder?
faqs.a: Yes — a hand-rolled ~60-line PNG-in-ICO writer. The favicon.ico file is a standard ICO header wrapping the 16×16 and 32×32 PNG blobs as separate frames. Every modern browser reads PNG-in-ICO files; Windows has supported them since Vista.

faqs.q: Why does my emoji look different on different machines?
faqs.a: Emoji are rendered with the user's system emoji font — Apple Color Emoji on macOS/iOS, Segoe UI Emoji on Windows, Noto Color Emoji on Linux/Chrome OS, etc. The PNGs in the zip will look like whatever your browser drew. If you need pixel-identical icons everywhere, drop in an SVG or PNG instead.

faqs.q: Does any of this leave my browser?
faqs.a: No. The image or emoji is rendered to a canvas locally, the PNGs and ICO are generated client-side, and the zip is assembled in your browser. Nothing is uploaded.

tools.name: UUID Generator
tools.card: Generate UUID v4 (random) or v7 (time-ordered) in bulk — copy individually or as a list.
tools.description: Generate UUID v4 (random) or v7 (time-ordered, monotonic) identifiers in bulk — copy individually or as a formatted list. Runs in your browser — no installs, no tracking.

faqs.q: What is the difference between UUID v4 and v7?
faqs.a: v4 is purely random — all 122 bits are random, giving no ordering information. v7 encodes a 48-bit millisecond timestamp in the first 6 bytes so UUIDs generated in the same millisecond are monotonically ordered. v7 is better for database primary keys where sequential insert order matters.

faqs.q: Is UUID v4 cryptographically secure?
faqs.a: Yes. The tool uses crypto.randomUUID() which is backed by the browser's cryptographically secure PRNG — the same source as crypto.getRandomValues().

faqs.q: Does the UUID v7 implementation follow the RFC?
faqs.a: Yes. It follows RFC 9562, encoding 48-bit millisecond timestamp, 4-bit version (7), 12-bit sequence counter for same-millisecond monotonicity, 2-bit variant, and 62-bit random bits.

faqs.q: Are these UUIDs unique?
faqs.a: With overwhelming statistical probability. The random bits in v4 give a collision probability of about 1 in 5.3 × 10^36 per pair. v7 adds a timestamp prefix making same-millisecond collisions even rarer. For practical purposes, treat them as unique.

faqs.q: Do any UUIDs leave my browser?
faqs.a: No. Generation uses only browser-native APIs (crypto.randomUUID, crypto.getRandomValues) and happens entirely locally — no server, no network, no tracking.

tools.name: SemVer Checker
tools.card: Check if a version satisfies a range — ^, ~, hyphen, wildcard, and more.
tools.description: Paste a version string and a range expression to instantly check whether the version satisfies the range, with a parsed breakdown and syntax cheat sheet. Runs in your browser, no tracking.

faqs.q: Which range operators are supported?
faqs.a: All standard npm semver operators: caret (^), tilde (~), hyphen ranges (1.0.0 - 2.0.0), wildcard (x, *), comparators (>, >=, <, <=, =), and OR chains (||). Pre-release identifiers and build metadata are also handled correctly.

faqs.q: Does my version string leave my browser?
faqs.a: No. Parsing and comparison happen entirely in your browser using the semver library bundled with the page — no upload, no server.

faqs.q: What does the range expansion show?
faqs.a: It normalises your input to its canonical comparator form, for example ^1.2.3 expands to >=1.2.3 <2.0.0. This makes it easy to understand exactly which versions a range allows.

faqs.q: Why does my pre-release version (e.g. 2.0.0-alpha.1) not satisfy ^1.0.0?
faqs.a: By default semver excludes pre-release versions from ranges unless the range explicitly includes a pre-release tag on the same [major, minor, patch] tuple. This matches npm's behavior.

faqs.q: Can I check multiple versions at once?
faqs.a: Not yet — the tool checks one version at a time. For batch checks, consider piping through the semver CLI in a terminal.

tools.name: JWT Decoder
tools.card: Decode JWT header, payload, and signature — timestamps shown as human-readable dates.
tools.description: Paste any JWT token to decode the header, payload, and signature — claim timestamps shown as human-readable dates, exp shows a live valid/expired badge. Runs in your browser — no installs, no tracking.

faqs.q: Does this verify the JWT signature?
faqs.a: No. Signature verification requires the secret key or the RSA/ECDSA public key, which the tool never has. The decoder only base64url-decodes the header and payload, which is safe and useful for inspecting contents without needing the key.

faqs.q: Is it safe to paste a real JWT here?
faqs.a: The decoding happens entirely in your browser — nothing is sent to a server. That said, JWTs can carry access tokens. Treat them like passwords: paste production tokens only in a trusted environment, and rotate any you paste into a public or shared machine.

faqs.q: What do the colour-coded token segments mean?
faqs.a: Red is the header (algorithm and type), purple is the payload (claims), and blue is the signature — the same colour convention used by jwt.io.

faqs.q: What is exp / nbf / iat?
faqs.a: exp (expiration) is the Unix timestamp after which the token is no longer valid. nbf (not before) is the earliest it should be accepted. iat (issued at) is when it was created. All three are rendered as human-readable UTC dates alongside the raw epoch value.

faqs.q: Does the tool support JWE or nested JWTs?
faqs.a: JWS compact serialisation (the common 3-part JWT) is supported. JWE (encrypted tokens, 5 parts) and nested JWTs are not decoded automatically — paste the inner token separately if needed.

tools.name: PDF Merger
tools.card: Combine multiple PDFs into one — reorder pages, pick page ranges, add bookmarks.
tools.description: Combine multiple PDFs (and optionally images) into a single file entirely in your browser. Drag to reorder, specify per-file page ranges, add bookmarks per source file, and strip metadata for privacy. No upload, no server, no tracking.

faqs.q: Do my PDFs ever leave my device?
faqs.a: No. All merging happens locally in your browser using pdf-lib and PDF.js — two open-source libraries that run entirely client-side. Your files are never uploaded anywhere.

faqs.q: Can I include only certain pages from each PDF?
faqs.a: Yes. Each file card has an optional Pages field. Leave it empty to include all pages, or type a range like '1-3, 7, 9-' (9- means page 9 through the last page).

faqs.q: What image formats can I drop in alongside PDFs?
faqs.a: PNG, JPEG, and WebP images are accepted. Each image is promoted to a single PDF page, sized to fit A4 (portrait) with the image centered.

faqs.q: What does 'Strip metadata' do?
faqs.a: It clears the Title, Author, Creator, and Producer fields from the output PDF. Useful when you want to share a document without leaking authoring details.

faqs.q: What does 'Add bookmarks per source' do?
faqs.a: It adds a top-level outline entry (bookmark) for each input file, pointing to the first page contributed by that file. This makes it easy to jump between source documents in any PDF viewer.
